clinical_record:
A 56-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of bitemporal hemianopia and left labial numbness. On examination, he had visual impairment, bitemporal hemianopia, and right abducens nerve palsy. Laboratory studies showed: TSH 0.658 μU/mL, free thyroxine 0.41 ng/dL, growth hormone 0.62 ng/mL, LH < 0.2 mIU/mL, FSH < 1.0 mIU/mL, prolactin 19.7 ng/mL, cortisol 0.5 μg/dL, ACTH 16.4 pg/mL, testosterone < 5.0 ng/dL, and IGF-1 119 ng/mL (−0.73 SD), consistent with hypopituitarism. Dynamic pituitary stimulation tests confirmed gonadotropin, thyroid, and adrenal axis deficiencies and severe GH deficiency. Serum IgG4 was elevated at 319 mg/dL (normal 4.8–105), with a normal total IgG of 1284 mg/dL (IgG4/IgG ratio 0.25).  
Pituitary MRI demonstrated diffuse swelling of the pituitary body and stalk, a 7-mm poorly enhancing mass in the right anterior lobe, loss of the posterior pituitary bright spot on T1-weighted images, and thickening of the sphenoid sinus mucosa. Chest CT revealed a nodular lesion in the left lung field, raising suspicion for systemic IgG4-related disease. No other organ involvement was identified on systemic imaging.  
Given the combination of hypopituitarism, elevated IgG4 levels, and imaging findings, the patient underwent endoscopic transnasal surgery of the pituitary gland for definitive diagnosis.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

candidate_registry.label: Metastatic disease to the pituitary gland

clinical_record:
A 27-year-old Japanese man presented with a 2-day history of posterior neck pain, sore throat, and odynophagia. He had no history of trauma, upper respiratory infection, or dental problems. On examination, active cervical range of motion was severely reduced by pain localized to the posterior neck. Oropharyngeal examination was normal, and there were no neurologic deficits. His temperature was 37.5°C. Laboratory tests showed a white-cell count of 12,500/mm³ and a C-reactive protein level of 1.0 mg/dL. A lateral cervical-spine radiograph revealed retropharyngeal thickening at the upper cervical spine and soft-tissue calcification anterior to the C1 arch. Unenhanced CT of the cervical spine demonstrated soft-tissue calcification extending from the longus colli muscle to the atlanto-odontoid joint.

A 29-year-old woman from the Dominican Republic, who moved to the United States in 2014, presented in January 2016 for prenatal care. A purified protein derivative skin test was positive (21 mm). In January 2022, she was started on rifampin (300 mg daily) for a planned 4-month course. She was taking no other medications. After three months of therapy, she experienced two days of nausea, vomiting, and subjective fevers.

Initial presentation showed no significant physical examination findings noted in the case report.

clinical_record:
A 34-year-old gravida 2, para 1 woman with a spontaneous dichorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy was transferred at 31 weeks 5 days’ gestation. Dichorionicity had been confirmed on first-trimester ultrasound. Pregnancy complications included early-onset growth restriction in twin 2 and new-onset preeclampsia at 30 weeks. At 16 weeks, ultrasound showed twin 1 with normal growth and normal amniotic fluid; twin 2 had estimated fetal weight <5th percentile, anhydramnios, and an absent bladder. Confirmatory ultrasound at 19 weeks revealed Tetralogy of Fallot in twin 2. By 21 weeks, twin 2’s amniotic fluid improved from anhydramnios to oligohydramnios (maximum vertical pocket 1.9 cm), and later normalized in both twins. Invasive testing was declined initially; at 31 weeks, chorionic villus sampling of twin 2 showed a normal chromosomal microarray.  
At 32 weeks, ultrasound at the tertiary center demonstrated:  
• Twin 1: estimated fetal weight 1904 g (62nd centile), normal amniotic fluid, normal umbilical-artery Dopplers, and middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity (MCA-PSV) 26 cm/s (0.56 multiples of the mean).  
• Twin 2: estimated fetal weight 1128 g (<5th centile), normal amniotic fluid, normal umbilical-artery Dopplers, and MCA-PSV 50.9 cm/s (1.3 MoM).  
Placental imaging showed a normal-appearing placenta for twin 1 and a thickened, echogenic placenta for twin 2. These findings prompted suspicion for twin anemia-polycythemia sequence and an emergency cesarean section at 32 + 2 weeks.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

candidate_registry.label: Considered genetic or chromosomal cause of growth restriction

clinical_record:
A 66-year-old woman with a history of endometrioid endometrial carcinoma presented with abdominal and pelvic pain. Physical examination was unremarkable, and laboratory studies, including a creatinine level of 0.81 mg dl–1, were within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a right renal mass with areas of fat attenuation located in the upper pole, creating a defect in the renal parenchyma. The lesion contained visible vessels extending into the renal cortex, a finding known as a “renal parenchymal vascular pedicle.” Additionally, there was a fatty tumor thrombus within the right renal vein extending to its confluence with the inferior vena cava. No other masses or enlarged lymph nodes were identified.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
